slides.text:
A variable gives a name to a value, and `let` creates one.

In Rust a variable is **read only** unless you say otherwise, and every value has a **type** that the compiler checks.

`println!` prints a line, and `{speed}` puts the variable `speed` in the text.
`let` creates a variable and gives it a value. By default it is **read only**: once it has a value, the compiler rejects a second assignment.
slides.code:
let speed = 10;

// speed = 20; does not compile

slides.text:
Write `mut` after `let` for a variable that has to change. Mark only the ones that need it, so the rest stay protected.

`lives -= 1` is the short form of `lives = lives - 1`, and the same works with `+=` and `*=`.

exercises.title: Change a value
exercises.guide: `count` goes up by one. Mark it so it can change.

exercises.title: Update a variable
exercises.guide: Make `total` changeable, then add `price` to it.

exercises.title: Update in place
exercises.guide: Double `level` with the short form of assignment.

slides.text: Every value has a type. Rust usually works it out, and you can write it after a colon. Whole numbers are `i8` to `i64` when they can be negative and `u8` to `u64` when they cannot. Decimals are `f64`.
A **constant** never changes, and its value is known when the program is built. Declare it with `const`, in capitals, and always write its type.

exercises.title: Name the type
exercises.guide: `year` is a whole number that fits in 32 bits and can be negative.

exercises.title: True, false and letters
exercises.guide: `ready` is a true or false value, and `letter` is a single character.

exercises.title: Whole and decimal
exercises.guide: `level` is a whole number from 0 to 255. `ratio` is a 64 bit decimal.

exercises.title: Declare a constant
exercises.guide: `MAX_LIVES` never changes while the program runs. Declare it.

exercises.title: Type of a constant
exercises.guide: A constant needs a type. Pick one that holds 86 400.

slides.text: A new `let` with a name that already exists **shadows** it: from there on, the old variable is hidden. Unlike `mut`, shadowing can also change the type that the name holds.
`as` converts a number to another type: `whole as f64` turns an integer into a float. Rust never converts between number types for you.
slides.code:
let whole: i32 = 3;
let decimal = whole as f64;

exercises.title: Shadow a variable
exercises.guide: Create a new `value`, one more than the old one, with no `mut`.

exercises.title: Change the type
exercises.guide: Replace `word` with its length. The name stays, the type changes.

exercises.title: Shadow, then change
exercises.guide: Shadow `total` with a changeable variable, then add 1 to it.

exercises.title: Convert a number
exercises.guide: Convert `count` to a float before the division.
